segments.say: Caring has a cost. Anyone who has looked after a sick relative, worked in a hospital or listened to a friend through a long crisis knows that helping can leave you drained. Psychologists have studied this, and have found that some forms of caring are far more draining than others. The difference may be the most useful thing in this whole video for people who help a lot.

In the 1970s and 1980s, a social psychologist named Christina Maslach began studying people who worked in caring jobs, such as nurses, social workers and teachers. She noticed a recurring pattern of exhaustion, cynicism and a sense of being ineffective. She called it burnout, and developed a questionnaire to measure it.

Christina Maslach and Susan Jackson described burnout as having three parts. Emotional exhaustion, the feeling of being drained. Depersonalisation, treating the people you help as objects or cases. And reduced personal accomplishment, a sense that nothing you do is making a difference. Their questionnaire became the most widely used measure in the field.

The second part is the one that surprises many people. When we are overwhelmed, we may protect ourselves by going numb, by seeing people as problems and not as individuals. It's not a moral failing. It's what overstretched minds sometimes do.

show.title: Three parts of burnout
items: Emotional exhaustion
Depersonalisation
Reduced sense of accomplishment
Often follows long stress without recovery

segments.say: In 1995, the psychologist Charles Figley edited a book describing what he called compassion fatigue: the emotional cost of caring for people who are suffering, particularly among those who work with trauma. It is related to burnout but focuses on the effect of absorbing other people's pain.

The key question for helpers is why some caring drains and some does not. A team led by Olga Klimecki and Tania Singer, then at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig, proposed an answer based on the difference between empathy and compassion.

show.title: Empathy and compassion are not the same

segments.say: These terms are used in different ways by different researchers, but in this research, empathy means sharing the other person's feelings, and compassion means feeling concern and the wish to help. They are different experiences, and they seem to involve different networks in the brain.

show.title: Two ways of responding to suffering
items: Empathy: feeling what the other person feels
Compassion: feeling warmth and concern for the other person
Empathy can lead to distress
Compassion can lead to motivation to help

segments.say: Klimecki and her colleagues trained adults for a short period in either empathy, learning to share others' feelings, or compassion, learning to generate feelings of warmth and care. Afterwards they watched videos of people suffering. Empathy training increased negative feelings, while compassion training increased positive feelings, and the two led to different patterns of brain activity.

show.what: Differential pattern of functional brain plasticity after compassion and empathy training

segments.say: The findings suggest that warm concern may be more sustainable than sharing every feeling. Compassion training seemed to counteract the negative effect of empathic distress. This was a short laboratory training, so the results are preliminary, but they fit what many carers say about how to last.

Four terms from this chapter. Burnout is exhaustion, cynicism and reduced effectiveness after long stress. Depersonalisation is treating people as objects. Compassion fatigue is the cost of absorbing others' suffering. And empathic distress is the pain of sharing another's pain.

show.title: Words to keep from this chapter
items: Burnout
Depersonalisation
Compassion fatigue
Empathic distress

segments.say: What helps? Research on burnout and recovery has found a few consistent ideas. They're not dramatic. They're the kind of things that tired people are tempted to skip.

These are ordinary points, but each has evidence behind it. Detaching from work in the evening, for example, has been linked to better recovery and wellbeing in studies of employees. The ability to switch off is a skill, and an important one.

show.title: What tends to protect helpers
items: Real breaks and sleep
Limits on how much one person carries
Support from colleagues or friends
A sense of meaning in the work
Time that has nothing to do with caring

segments.say: Sabine Sonnentag and Charlotte Fritz identified four experiences that help people to recover from work: psychological detachment, relaxation, mastery experiences and a sense of control over leisure time. People who reported more of these tended to report better wellbeing. The same ideas apply to unpaid carers.

show.what: The Recovery Experience Questionnaire: development and validation of a measure for assessing recuperation and unwinding from work

segments.say: It can feel selfish to rest when someone needs you. The research suggests the opposite. Someone who is exhausted helps less well, and for less time. Rest is part of how helping continues, and not a betrayal of it.

If you recognise these, please speak to a doctor or a counsellor. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, contact an emergency service or a crisis line in your country. Needing help while helping others is common, and it's nothing to be ashamed of.

show.title: A note on when to seek support
items: Persistent exhaustion that sleep does not fix
Feeling numb or dreading the people you care for
Trouble sleeping or eating
Thoughts of harming yourself

segments.say: Here is a small plan for any person who helps a lot. Choose one evening with no caring tasks. Tell someone you trust how you are really doing. Do one thing that is only for you. And ask for one specific piece of help. Picture this scene: a woman who looks after her father every day asks her brother to take Thursday evenings. He agrees at once. He had been waiting to be asked. She spends her first free Thursday on a bench with a book, and finds she cannot concentrate, because she has forgotten how to rest. By the third week, she can. The help she gave was no smaller. It was better supported.

show.title: A small plan for the week
items: Choose one evening with no caring tasks
Tell someone you trust how you are
Do one thing that is only for you
Ask for one specific piece of help

segments.say: A pause, especially for people who care for others a great deal. How tired are you, honestly? Not tired in the polite sense, but in the sense of being worn thin. Think about what you carry for other people: a parent, a child, a team, a friend in crisis. Who could share the load? Many carers say they find it hard to ask, partly because they fear being a burden and partly because they've forgotten what rest feels like. The research on burnout is clear that this isn't a personal weakness, and that recovery needs real breaks and real support. Is there one thing you could stop, delay or hand over? It might be small. Even a single evening, a single task, a single conversation postponed can ease the pressure. Looking after the helper isn't a luxury. It is how the help continues.

show.title: Pause and reflect
items: How tired am I, honestly?
What do I carry for other people?
Who could share the load?
What is one thing I could stop or delay?

segments.say: A lantern burning low, with a blanket folded beside it. A light needs fuel to keep burning, and the research on helpers suggests the same of people. Caring can last, if it is fed. We ended this chapter on rest on purpose. A culture that praises helpers while ignoring their tiredness loses them. The research says that care and recovery belong together, and that looking after yourself is not selfish.

If you are the person everyone leans on, remember that you're also a person. The studies of helpers are clear: care that lasts includes care for the one giving it. Looking after yourself is part of looking after others.

So what did we learn? That burnout has three parts, including numbness and a sense of ineffectiveness. That empathy and compassion are different and have different effects. That warm concern may be more sustainable. And that real rest is part of helping well.
In the next chapter, we'll bring the research together into a simple map of the steps that stand between seeing a need and meeting it.
